books.section: Topic 3.12 Movement in the Early Republic

primary_sources: George Caleb Bingham, Daniel Boone Escorting Settlers through the Cumberland Gap, 1851-52

stimulus.text: George Caleb Bingham, Daniel Boone Escorting Settlers through the Cumberland Gap, 1851–52. The painting shows a man in buckskin carrying a rifle, leading a white horse with a woman rider, followed by armed settlers and a dog, through a rocky mountain pass. Background from the books: Daniel Boone blazed the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap in 1775, opening a path for settlers into Kentucky.
stimulus.source_note: George Caleb Bingham, Daniel Boone Escorting Settlers through the Cumberland Gap, 1851-52, oil on canvas, Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum, Washington University in St. Louis. Public domain. Image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — George Caleb Bingham, Daniel Boone Escorting Settlers through the Cumberland Gap, 1851-52. Public domain.
stem: Why would a painter in the 1850s show Boone as a heroic guide leading whole families westward?

options.text: To record the exact clothing and weapons the settlers carried in 1775.
options.misconception: A later painting cannot record exact details from 1775.

options.text: To celebrate westward movement as a proud American story.
To warn settlers that the mountain pass was too dangerous to cross.
options.misconception: The settlers walk calmly forward in bright light, not in danger or retreat.

options.text: To protest the government's sale of western land at auction.
options.misconception: Nothing in the painting concerns land sales or prices.

rationales.A: Bingham painted in the 1850s, so he could not record 1775 details firsthand.
rationales.B: Background: in the 1850s Americans were still moving west. Bingham therefore pictured Boone as a hero leading families to honor that movement in his own day.
rationales.C: The group walks forward in light, not away from danger.
rationales.D: The painting shows a journey, not a land sale.
rationales.general:
1. Background: the painting was made in the 1850s, when westward movement was still under way.
2. Boone stands in bright light at the head of the line, calm and sure.
3. The families behind him follow without fear.
4. So the picture honors westward movement for the painter's own time as much as it recalls 1775.
Remember: a picture about the past also speaks to the time it was made.
